title: Walk Reach Radius: The 15-Minute Circle
description: Draw the walkable reach around a point with the Walk Reach Radius — 5, 10 and 15-minute circles at honest walking speeds. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, at a typical 3 mph pace, 15 minutes of walking is a 0.75-mile radius covering 1.77 square miles — the famous '15-minute neighbourhood', drawn as the circle it actually is.
quick_answer: The Walk Reach Radius draws the area reachable on foot around a point, using walking time and an honest pace — about 3 miles per hour for most adults. Choose 5, 10, 15 or 20 minutes and read the circle — the first-pass walkability map streets later refine.
steps_intro: Time times pace equals reach — draw it:

body.t: Planners' slogan, made measurable: what falls inside a quarter-hour's walk of a home or station? The overlay tools count contents; this page draws the honest circle first.
'Walkable' in a listing becomes a radius around the address — checkable in one drawing, before the viewing.
Walking catchments for schools and clinics start as reach circles; policy draws the final line, but the circle is the evidence base.
A hotel's 10-minute circle is the visitor's real city — sights inside it are today's plan; the rest is tomorrow's bus.

At 3 mph, 15 minutes reaches 0.75 mi; at a brisk 4 mph, a full mile — the circle's area grows by 78% (1.77 → 3.14 sq mi). State the pace next to any walkability claim; the claim is meaningless without it.

Streets rarely run straight at the destination: real walking reach is the circle eroded by the network, often 60–80% of it. The radius map is the ceiling; network tools draw the true shape — and honest pages say which they are showing.

popular_table.title: Walking reach at 3 mph
popular_table.intro: The standard pace (20 minutes per mile) — computed circles.
popular_table.note: Pace varies — children, hills, heat and age all edit it. The table's 3 mph is the planning standard, adjustable in the tool; what matters is that the pace travels with the claim.

faq: Does it follow sidewalks and paths?
No — this is the straight-line reach circle, the honest first pass. Network-based walk sheds are the refinement; the circle is the ceiling they can never exceed.
What pace for children or older walkers?
About 2–2.5 mph is the kinder planning pace — select it and the circle shrinks to the walker's real world, which is the respectful way to plan.
Gradient eats pace (Naismith's rule adds time for ascent). Flat-circle reach in hill country overstates; treat the drawing as the best case there.
At 4 mph yes; at the standard 3 mph it is 0.75 miles. The slogan survives because brisk walkers exist — the tool lets the pace be chosen rather than assumed.
Multiply pace by roughly four (12 mph) and the same drawing serves — the tool's pace input covers it, labelled as cycling when used so.
Overlay question — the buffer tools count what's inside; this page draws how far the feet reach.
Reach is geometry; comfort is another layer (lighting, crossings) no radius draws. Planners pair the circle with the street audit.
The 15-minute city was coined in Paris — km circles are this tool's native second language.
